rationale: The two pediatric clinical cases describe a different neurological condition. One case includes visual and auditory hallucinations during illness. This is clinical context for differential interpretation, with no Parkinson disease cohort or food comparison.

The clinical report describes visual and auditory hallucinations in a child with multiple sclerosis. Its population and observation do not address idiopathic Parkinson disease, recurrent visual event frequency or dried-fig intake.

The report synthesizes a series of controlled Tourette syndrome comparisons. The text refers to hallucinations in contextual comparisons, including descriptions from other disorders. Its own group comparison does not measure Parkinson visual hallucination frequency or dried-fig intake.

The article studies movement abnormalities in a mouse model. Its introduction separately recounts a previously published human case of acute illness with visual hallucinations and parkinsonian features, attributed to Richter and colleagues. The human observation is a citation in the background. It adds no independently observed Parkinson cases, food exposure or visual episode rate to the animal paper.

Lloyd describes visual hallucinations in severe delirium and distinguishes symptoms arising during Parkinson therapy from symptoms attributable to disease. This is clinical diagnostic context. No separate visual episode rate or dried-fig comparison is reported.

Quinn describes visual hallucination history in diffuse Lewy body disease. The review also cites a comparison in which visual hallucinations and fluctuations were as common in pure Alzheimer disease, qualifying how specifically those symptoms distinguished diagnoses in the cited evidence. The source supplies diagnostic history without a new patient sample, a visual episode-frequency measure or dried-fig exposure.

Quinn distinguishes visual illusions, perceived presence, experiences with retained insight, and visual hallucinations. The review discusses psychotic symptoms during motor off periods and dietary protein in the context of levodopa response and motor fluctuations. The dietary discussion supplies no evidence for dried figs or a visual episode-rate comparison.

Amar and Wilcock contrast vascular dementia with other dementias, including dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia. The diagnostic box uses early prominent visual hallucinations as one contextual feature. The review reports no new symptom-frequency or dried-fig comparison.
